thread.title: How to Lower Your Stock-Market Risk Ahead of the Election

author: Gunjan Banerji
title: How to Lower Your Stock-Market Risk Ahead of the Election
text:
Nikhita Singhal By Gunjan Banerji Updated Sept. 28, 2018 6:19 p.m. ET Hints of election jitters are emerging in the options market.
Though markets have calmed and U.S. stock indexes are edging toward record highs once again, some signals indicate investors are gearing for greater turbulence in coming weeks. One point of focus: the Nov. 6 midterm elections, which will determine whether Democrats are able to wrangle control of Congress. Republicans currently hold a slim majority in both houses.
No matter what, investors should be aware that betting on election outcomes is risky. Often political shifts don’t have the market implications many project, as was on display in the 2016 presidential election. Moreover, outcomes can be wide-ranging and tough to forecast.
Still, futures contracts tracking the Cboe Volatility Index , or VIX, that expire in October have jumped relatively high compared with the so-called fear gauge’s level over the past week, reflecting anxiety ahead of the election, said Pravit Chintawongvanich, an equity derivatives strategist at Wells Fargo Securities, in a Sept. 25 note.
The October futures contracts are calculated through S&P 500 options expiring in the next month and could stay elevated, he says. Meanwhile, weekly options bets on the S&P 500 have already been reflecting heightened turbulence around that time, indicating investors are bracing for a bigger move than usual for the week starting Nov. 2, according to Wells Fargo.
“Markets still remain very fragile,” Benjamin Bowler, global head of equity derivatives research at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, told Barron’s. “When you see shocks, they tend to be more violent.”
Though the recent move lower for volatility could be an indicator to some that little has changed this year from last year—when an epic calm blanketed markets —there have been shifts under the surface.
For example, the average move lower for the S&P 500 has been 0.7% this year, compared with 0.3% in 2017, according to the Dow Jones Market Data Group as of Thursday. Meanwhile, global stocks have swung wildly.
To be sure, some investors continue to tap bullish call options in anticipation of another leg higher in the S&P 500, analysts note. Call options give investors the right to buy shares at a given price and time.
A rise in Treasury yields helped push stocks into a tailspin earlier this year, but the recent move higher for government bond yields—and the accompanying fall in prices—hasn’t precipitated the same cross-asset swings. U.S. stock indexes recently broke records and equity volatility receded.
Investors looking to pare some risk through the rest of the year could replace existing stock exposure with options contracts, says Don Dale, a managing member of Equity Risk Control Group. He says that because realized volatility—or what markets have actually experienced—has been low, call options look like a decent bargain at the moment.
Newsletter Sign-up Dale recommends replacing large-cap technology stocks with options, such as call options on the Invesco QQQ Trust exchange-traded fund (ticker: QQQ).
Investors could tap call options with a $190 strike price expiring in January, which cost $520 per contract as of Thursday. Each contract covers 100 shares of the fund. Currently, investors aren’t pricing in large swings for the fund through January, making it a better value, Dale says. This would give investors the right to buy the fund if it hits that level by January but also protect them from a potential swoon in their outstanding stock exposure, he says.
The fund has advanced almost 20% this year and holds heavyweights like Apple (AAPL) and Nvidia (NVDA). It closed Thursday at $185.83, up 0.85%.
Gunjan Banerji covers options for The Wall Street Journal.
